label: Evidence-informed reasoning — Specific NMC811 pouch-cell target
question: Propose an evidence-supported starting fast-charge protocol for a 5 Ah graphite/NMC811 pouch cell at 25 °C, charging from 10% to 80% SOC with a target time of 20 minutes while limiting lithium plating. Give current stages and transition criteria only when supported, and clearly identify values that cannot be determined from the evidence.

conditions.objective: target 20 minutes while limiting lithium plating

what_it_tests: Evidence-informed reasoning: whether the system produces one usable experimental starting protocol while distinguishing reported values, evidence-informed transfer, engineering judgment, and unresolved parameters.

answer.summary: Evidence supports a conservative, experimentally testable fast-charge starting protocol for a graphite/NMC811 5 Ah pouch cell at 25 °C, but not a fully reported protocol for the exact target. The literature most directly supports the design direction: high current at low SOC, reduced current at higher SOC, and a voltage ceiling near 4.1 V for plating avoidance in a related graphite/NMC cell. Because the exact chemistry, capacity, and SOC window are not directly reported, the current values below are engineering judgments informed by related studies.

protocol_suggestions.rationale: The protocol is synthesized from three evidence threads. First, graphite/NMC fast-charge literature indicates that current should be higher at low SOC and lower at higher SOC to reduce lithium-plating risk; model work also favors multi-step CCCV or voltage-ramping concepts over a single high-current stage. Second, a graphite/NMC model study states that a 5C+CC stage should be terminated below 4.1 V for a 2.5 mAh cm^-2 cell to avoid plating, which is the closest directly stated voltage ceiling available. Third, a large pouch-cell current map shows that allowable current decreases strongly as SOC rises, supporting a two-stage structure rather than a single constant current. Because no cited source directly reports a 5 Ah graphite/NMC811 pouch-cell protocol at 25 °C from 10% to 80% SOC, the current magnitudes and the 4.2 V upper bound in Stage 2 are experimental assumptions rather than reported values.

Conclusions
Based on the features of the semi-optimal protocol, two practical novel fast charging protocols were proposed, namely the voltage ramping protocol and the multiple CCCV protocol. The simulation results showed that for the 2.5 mAh cm -2 cell, the maximum capacity after 10 min charge at 30 °C without lithium plating can be improved by up to 10.7% using the proposed protocols compared with the standard CCCV protocol. To achieve 80% charge in 10 min, the proposed protocols will require a charging temperature that is 8 °C lower than that of the CCCV protocol, which minimizes parasitic reactions and prolongs battery life. Finally, we predicted that the proposed protocols are more effective for the fast charging of high loading cells. For a 4 mAh cm -2 cell, the proposed protocols can improve the charge rate by up to 18.8% without lithium plating according to model prediction.
While this work only considered the driving force for lithium plating of a fresh cell as the optimization metric, other degradation mechanisms such as loss of lithium inventory, loss of active materials and increase of cell resistance can be taken into account in a similar manner. Also, these degradation mechanisms may change the lithium plating behavior of the cell, which necessitates adjusting the fast charge protocol as the cell ages. These will be the topics of our future work. Finally, results reported in this article are based on simulation only. Experimental validation of the proposed fast charging protocols is ongoing to verify their improved extreme fast charging capability and cycle life over traditional protocols.

Fast Charging of Li-Ion Cells: Part V. Design and Demonstration of Protocols to Avoid Li-Plating
Ilya A. Shkrob, Marco-Tulio F. Rodrigues, and Daniel P. Abraham * ,z
Chemical Sciences and Engineering Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, Illinois 60439, United States of America
ECS
Fast charging of Li-ion batteries would make ' fueling ' of electric vehicles comparable in time to fueling of gasoline-powered cars, increasing consumer appeal of the new technology. Taking the US Department of Energy goal of safe 6 C charging to 80% capacity as a guide, we describe approaches that can mitigate Li plating on the graphite anode. To make this possible, a variable-rate anode potential charging protocol has been implemented by using a microprobe reference electrode to continuously monitor and adjust the current, in this way avoiding low anode potentials that favor Li deposition. Various implementations of the anode potential control are considered using electrochemical modeling and compared with the experimental data. For charge to 80% capacity at 30 °C, an average C-rate of 4.97 C was obtained for an NCM523/graphite cell with 70 μ mthick graphite electrode and 7.40 C for a cell with 47 μ m thick graphite electrode. Our electrochemical model accounts for these observations and provides a means to extrapolate the approach to other cell designs and operation regimes, drawing the maximum average fast charging rates that can still avoid Li plating.

Experimental
Table I lists the material, electrode, cell design parameters, and Table II includes the charging protocols. Graphite (1506T Superior Graphite) and NMC532 (Toda America) were used as respective negative and positive electrode active materials, respectively, to fabricate electrodes at the Cell Analysis, Modeling, and Prototyping (CAMP) Facility at Argonne National Laboratory (Argonne). These electrodes were cut and assembled in single layer pouch cells with Celgard 2320 separator. 1.2 M LiPF6 in a 3:7 by wt. ethylene carbonate: ethylmethyl carbonate electrolyte was used. The reversible capacity of the negative electrode and positive electrode at C/10 were measured to be 1.93 mAh cm -2 and 1.65 mAh cm -2 using half cells. The reversible negative to positive capacity ratio (N: P ratio) was set at 1.17 for C/10 rate (1.26 for C/1) by adjusting the mass loading of the electrodes for the operating cell voltage window of 3-4.1V. The cells were built such that the footprint of the negative electrode overhung the edge of the positive electrode by 0.5 mm on all sides. Such oversize accommodates slight imperfections of electrode alignment during cell assembly and avoid preferential plating of Li at the edges by guaranteeing there is Gr material directly opposite of the cathode.

Results and Discussion
The shown fast charge protocol allows a charging of the cell from 0%SoC to 85%SoC in 26.8 min. To validate the developed charging protocol three cells were cycled with this protocol. Start condition was 25 °C ±1 °C cell temperature and the temperature of the chamber held constant. Cells were cycled in the already presented test setup (refer to Fig. 1) to realize the same test conditions as in second test case. The cycling was started at 0%SoC and the cell was charged with the optimized protocol. Afterwards for relaxation a waiting time of 1 h with following discharge with 1/3 C to 0%SoC has been done. Followed by a further relaxation phase of 2 h. This procedure was repeated for 100 cycles with a capacity check every 25 cycles. After these 100 cycles the state of health (short SoH) of tested cells compared to initial capacity was over 95% and no abnormalities (for example voltage shoulder during relaxation phase) during whole test time occurred. In comparison cycling the cells with same test procedure from 0% to 80% SoC with a constant charging current of 1/3 C at 25 °C for 100 cycles, show a discharge capacity loss of not even 4%, means a SoH of over 96%. During this test about 95% of the Ah throughput for the 100 cycles in comparison to 100 fast charge cycles has been done. Based on the comparison of capacity retention after 100cycles from both tests no abnormal capacity loss based on fast charging could be shown.

Conclusions
In this work, the Pseudo2D electrochemical battery model was used to screen traditional fast charging protocols for a moderate HEV loading (2.5 mAh cm -2 ) graphite/NMC 532 cell. The simulation results showed that in terms of the maximum driving force for lithium plating, CCCV and CPCV protocols outperform the multistage constant-current charging with a single voltage cutoff and the pulse charging. To prevent lithium plating, the 5C + constant-current charging stage should be terminated at a voltage lower than 4.1 V for the investigated 2.5 mAh cm -2 cell. A fast charging algorithm was developed that charges the cell at close-to-maximum current at all time without causing lithium plating. The resultant semi-optimal protocol further illustrated that to achieve fast charging without lithium plating, the cell should be charged at a higher current when the cell voltage is low, and charged to higher voltage when the charge current is low.

4. Conclusion
An online optimal fast charging method was proposed based on a reduced electrochemical model that embeds submodels for side reaction, lithium plating and stripping as a function of temperature. The experimentally validated models are used to analyze the effects of Crates and temperature on the side reaction and lithium plating and then find out the optimal temperatures at different C-rates. At the optimal temperatures, the battery has the longest cycling life. Then, the nonlinear model predictive control is used to determine charging currents and operating temperatures. In order to recover the ions out of the plated lithium, pulse discharging currents are added to the charging protocol to promote the lithium stripping, where the amplitude and frequency of the discharging current are also optimized using the validated model. Finally, the method and traditional CC/CV charging methods were implemented into a Battery-In-the-Loop system and assessed with respect to charging time and cycle life, where the temperature was actively controlled by a designed thermostat system to track the optimal temperatures. The test results have verified that the protocol can reduce the charging time and extends the cycle life.
Here is a summary of major findings;
- When the operating temperature is high, the side reaction is accelerated, but the lithium plating becomes slowed down. Conversely, at low temperatures, the side reaction rate becomes less but the lithium plating rate increases.

Discussion
It should be noted that at high temperature other degradation mechanisms may be more signi fi cant than lithium plating. It is not well understood what temperature is acceptable for the fast charging process. If the battery can be warmed and cooled in a few minutes, then fast charging may be carried out at relatively high temperature without much detrimental lifetime effects/SEI damage. This has been demonstrated 16 in low capacity cells with modest energy density where temperature is easily modulated, but whether this can be done in large capacity packs is the subject of debate. The simulation results reported in this Section shows that temperature alone, even a very high one of 55 °C, does not enable good capacity in 10 min for an EV type cell. 8,36 Instead, a combination of very high temperature and novel protocol is needed to achieve capacity. If it is determined that the charging temperature must be lowered, the proposed protocol is still bene fi cial because it lowers the amount of improvements needed for electrolyte transport/electrode tortuosity, which are costly to improve.
While this subsection only investigates the effectiveness of the voltage ramping protocol on the fast charging of a high loading cell, one can infer that the multi-CCCV protocol can achieve similar maximum no-plating capacity as the voltage ramping protocol. However, several CCCV steps are likely needed as the higher loading cell is more prone to lithium plating, increasing implementation complexity compared to the voltage ramping protocol.

In this series of papers 1 -4 we examine the practical limits of fast charging for Li-ion cells built of commercially available materials. 5 -10 We are particularly interested in preventing lithium plating on the graphite anode, which is endemic to this material: strong cell polarization at high currents leads the anode potential to decrease to values at which Li plating becomes competitive with Li intercalation, causing severe performance loss. 11 As this damage can be extensive, 10 fast charging regimes that avoid Li plating are required.

4. Conclusion
- Active variation of operating temperature along with current profiles optimized by nonlinear model predictive control significantly enables extension of cycle life by suppressing side reaction and lithium plating.
- Since pulse discharging current promotes the lithium stripping and recovers ions out of the plated lithium, a higher charging current can be applied than that commonly derived by limiting the overpotential to prevent lithium plating. Therefore, the charging time is further reduced without imposing any penalty on capacity fade.
- The charging time is reduced 61% and 39% (1 C CC/CV) and 32% and 9% (2 C CC/CV) up to 80% and 100% SOC, respectively, while the capacity fade is comparable and 71% less up to 220 cycles, respectively.

2.5. CC -CV Reference Charging
As a reference for both fast charging procedures aging cycles with 1 C charge current were conducted (see Figure 2). Here, the cells were charged with 1 C CC to the maximum cell voltage of 4.2 V followed by a CV phase to C/20. Afterward, the cells were www.entechnol.de discharged again with 1 C CC to 3 V. Between charge and discharge steps, there were always 10 min rest periods.
After aging testing, selected cells were discharged to 3 V and opened in an argon-filled glovebox. The cell components were separated and dried overnight in vacuum without further treatment. No additional washing with solvents was done to preserve the surface of the electrode. Following this, the anodes were transported in a closed box to a scanning electron microscope (ZEISS Gemini) for surface analysis. There, the samples were inserted into the electron microscope. The samples spent several minutes in ambient air.
